extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in CS103 / discrete structures (proofwriting practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and templates for writing formal proofs about objects and statements expressed in first-order logic (e.g., proving injectivity, surjectivity, bijections, and manipulating quantifiers). Intended as a how-to handout for discrete-structures problem sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match proof structure to first-order logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement is specified in first-order logic, look at its logical structure (quantifiers/connectives) and use that to decide how to structure the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a universally-quantified statement suggests picking arbitrary elements; an implication suggests assuming the antecedent; a mixed ∀∃ suggests pick arbitrary outer variable then produce an inner witness. This principle underlies all the given templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving ∀x. P (universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct: Pick an arbitrary x, then prove P for that x. By contradiction: assume there exists some x where P is false and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a universal, explicitly choose an arbitrary representative and prove P about it. The 'by contradiction' route negates the universal to an existential and is less common but valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving ∃x. P (existential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct: Find and produce a specific choice of x that satisfies P and justify why it works. Proofs by contradiction for existential statements are extremely rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must give a concrete witness and show P holds for it. Expect exploratory work (examples, pictures) to discover a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving ¬P (negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct: Simplify by pushing negation inward and apply appropriate rules. By contradiction: assume P and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat negation by rewriting into equivalent first-order form or use contradiction as standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving P ∧ Q (conjunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct: Prove P and prove Q independently. By contradiction: assume ¬P ∨ ¬Q and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State you will prove each conjunct, and present independent subproofs for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving P ∨ Q (disjunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct: Prove either ¬P → Q or ¬Q → P (i.e., show one disjunct holds by proving the contrapositive of the other). By contradiction: assume ¬P ∧ ¬Q and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand truth-table intuition. One common direct tactic is to assume the negation of one disjunct and show the other must hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving P → Q (implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct: Assume P and prove Q. By contradiction: assume P and ¬Q and derive a contradiction. By contrapositive: assume ¬Q and prove ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the approach that best fits available information (direct introduction of antecedent, contradiction, or contrapositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving P ↔ Q (biconditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove both directions P → Q and Q → P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as two separate implication proofs; you may use rules above for each direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming ∀x. P (using a universal hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you assume a universal statement, do not introduce arbitrary variables immediately; instead, wait until a specific object z arises and then instantiate the universal to conclude P(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do nothing initially. Think of ∀x. P as a tool you can apply when you 'find a nail' (a specific z). Do not treat the universal assumption like a concrete choice of x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming ∃x. P (using an existential hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assuming an existential, introduce a new variable that has property P and use it in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You get a witness 'for free' when assuming an existential; e.g., from 'n is even' you may assume there exists k with n = 2k and use k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming ¬P
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace assuming ¬P by negating P and then consult the rules for that syntactic form (e.g., push negation inward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table to see what internal assumptions result from the negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming P ∧ Q
rubrics_metrics.description: When assuming a conjunction, assume both P and Q are true and use them freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as having both pieces of information available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming P ∨ Q (when using a disjunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed by cases: consider one case where P is true and another where Q is true, and show the desired conclusion follows in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure your proof with explicit case analysis; ensure both cases are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming P → Q (using an implication hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initially do nothing; later, if you find that P holds, you may conclude Q. Do not immediately assume P just because the implication is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat implication as a conditional tool to be invoked when antecedent is established; don't gratuitously assume antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming P ↔ Q (using a biconditional hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume both directions P → Q and Q → P and use the rules for implications; alternatively, do case analysis on (P and Q) and (¬P and ¬Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either treat as two implications or do cases where both hold or both fail, depending on convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijection proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove f : A → B is a bijection, prove injectivity and surjectivity separately (i.e., show f is injective and f is surjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the proof as two mini-proofs labeled 'injective' and 'surjective'. If f is a concrete, previously-defined object, do not restate its definition at the start of the proof; if f is arbitrary, explicitly introduce it first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity proof template (definition 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove f is injective using the form ∀x1 ∀x2 (f(x1)=f(x2) → x1 = x2): pick arbitrary x1,x2 ∈ A, assume f(x1) = f(x2), and show x1 = x2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand whatever definition or properties of f you have; if f is concrete, plug in its rule. Do not repeat the external definition of f inside the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity proof template (equivalent definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove f is injective using the form ∀x1 ∀x2 (x1 ≠ x2 → f(x1) ≠ f(x2)): pick arbitrary x1,x2 ∈ A, assume x1 ≠ x2, and show f(x1) ≠ f(x2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same practical rules apply; choose whichever definition fits your available information better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving not injective (negation / counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negate the injectivity definition to get ∃x1 ∃x2 (x1 ≠ x2 ∧ f(x1) = f(x2)). To show f is not injective, produce specific x1 and x2 satisfying these conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existential proofs require concrete witnesses—explicitly define x1 and x2 and justify both x1 ≠ x2 and f(x1) = f(x2). The hard part is finding the witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity proof template
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove f : A → B is surjective, use ∀b ∈ B ∃a ∈ A f(a) = b: pick an arbitrary b ∈ B, then construct a specific a ∈ A (a witness) and show f(a) = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One step is outside your control (arbitrary b); the other is constructive (choose a). If f is concrete use its definition; if not, use given properties of f to produce a suitable a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not restate external definitions inside proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If an object (function, set, etc.) is explicitly defined outside the proof, do not repeat its definition at the top of your proof; use it directly instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions: keep proofs concise by referencing previously given definitions. If proving a universally-quantified claim about arbitrary objects, introduce the arbitrary object explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formal logical notation in prose proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though definitions may be given in first-order logic, a written proof should use plain English (no quantifier/connective syntax) while following the logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., pick arbitrary elements and say 'we assume...' rather than writing ∀ or → inside the main prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining functions: required pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a function you must give the domain and codomain and a rule explaining how to evaluate the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Consider f : ℕ → ℕ defined by f(n) = n+1.' For complex behavior use piecewise definitions, ensuring all cases are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining functions: piecewise and combined definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Piecewise: specify behavior in each case and (internally) make sure all cases are covered. Combining: you may define functions by composition (e.g., let h = g ∘ f) with no further elaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For piecewise definitions, verify case coverage on your own even if not spelled out in the written proof. For finite-domain examples, pictures are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative diagrams for finite-domain functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For functions with finite domain and codomain you may define them by diagramming domain, codomain, and arrows instead of giving a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to show existence of functions with a given property (e.g., a doubly-covered map) where enumerating all values is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs by cases and using lemmas for longer proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer or multipart proofs, break the argument into lemmas (smaller proofs) that are proven separately and invoked in the main theorem to keep the main proof concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label lemmas clearly; the distinction between lemma and theorem is contextual. Use lemmas to offload technical subarguments or to handle independent parts of a larger proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential witness-finding is exploratory
rubrics_metrics.description: When an existential must be proven (e.g., not injective, surjectivity witness), be prepared to try examples, draw pictures, and experiment to find suitable witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The write-up shows the chosen witnesses and justification; the discovery process is often informal and exploratory.
